query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Heat treatment that induces enhanced short‐range ordering among chromium and other alloying elements in stainless steels promotes the formation of a more continuous and protective Cr‐oxide passive film, thereby reducing localized corrosion in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional stainless steel with a typical, random distribution of alloying elements (e.g., Cr, Ni, Mo) in its microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat treatment designed to promote short-range ordering of the alloying elements without altering the bulk composition.
generation.conditions: Test samples are exposed to environments that simulate aggressive chemical-processing media (e.g., saline or acidic solutions) and, where feasible, aspects of nuclear-power conditions (e.g., elevated temperatures and moderate radiation levels).
generation.structural_mediator: The development of nanoscale clusters or ordered domains enriched in chromium (and/or synergistic elements) that serve as uniform nucleation sites for the formation of a stable, protective Cr-oxide film at the steel surface.
generation.mechanism: By reducing random elemental distribution, the induced short-range ordering minimizes regions deficient in Cr, leading to a more uniform passivation layer. This layer helps to suppress localized corrosion processes such as pitting, by maintaining barrier integrity even under corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with a baseline of conventionally annealed (random distribution) steels, the heat-treated, short-range-ordered steels will exhibit lower corrosion rates, fewer pit initiation sites, and improved long-term passivity in aggressive environments.
generation.baseline: Standard stainless steel processing without the specialized heat treatment yields a random microstructure that forms a less uniformly protective passive film, resulting in relatively higher corrosion rates.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for steels with sufficient chromium content (typically ≥12%) under corrosive conditions representative of chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments. The benefit of short-range ordering may not extend to steels with very high impurity levels or those undergoing significant mechanical damage that disrupts the passive film.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how much of the observed corrosion resistance is exclusively due to short-range ordering versus other microstructural factors (such as grain boundary character, residual stresses, or inclusions). Additional studies are needed to isolate these variables.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two identical sets of stainless steel samples with the same composition. Subject one set to the specific heat treatment meant to promote short-range ordering and leave the other set untreated. Expose both sets to identical corrosive environments (e.g., 3.5% NaCl solution and/or mildly acidic media) under controlled temperature conditions. Monitor the formation and stability of the passive film over time.
measurements: Potentiodynamic polarization curves to quantify corrosion rates.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to assess passive film stability.
Weight loss measurements over a fixed period.
Microscopic and spectroscopic analysis (e.g., SEM, EDS, XPS) to characterize the uniformity and composition of the passive oxide layer.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated steel shows no statistically significant improvement—or exhibits worse performance—in terms of corrosion rate, pit density, and passive film integrity compared to the untreated steel, then the hypothesis that short-range ordering is principally responsible for enhanced corrosion resistance is falsified.

Microstructure, Thermal, and Corrosion Behavior of the AlAgCuNiSnTi Equiatomic Multicomponent Alloy

Abstract: AbstractThe paper presents the microstructure and corrosion behavior of an AlTiNiCuAgSn new equiatomic multicomponent alloy. The alloy was obtained using the vacuum arc remelting (VAR) technique in MRF-ABJ900 equipment. The microstructural analysis was performed by optical and scanning electron microscopy (SEM microscope, SEM-EDS) and the phase transformations were highlighted by dilatometric analysis and differential thermal analysis (DTA). The results show that the as-cast alloy microstructure is three-phase, with an average microhardness of 487 HV0.1/15. The obtained alloy could be included in the group of compositionally complex alloys (CCA). The corrosion resistance was studied using the potentiodynamic method in saline solution with 3.5% NaCl. Considering the high corrosion resistance, the obtained alloy can be used for surface coating applications.Keywords: high entropy alloy, equiatomic multicomponent alloy, microstructure, corrosion resistance, surface coatings
